author: Nick Cox
title: Of all the comments about Q1 2018 results for Apple (NASDAQ:
text:
Of all the comments about Q1 2018 results for Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL ) many analysts have not emphasized how strongly Apple is performing in Asia. My article in December predicted Apple's results would show stronger growth in Asia than anticipated. So it turned out. This shows how Asia will become increasingly important to the company and be the single strongest growth driver in coming years.
Q1 2018 in Asia. An analysis of the company's results illustrate the growth from Asia.
The unaudited data summary shows this in relation to revenue as below:

The net sales by reportable segment is as follows:

The figures are striking.
In terms of revenue year-on-year:
Americas + 10%
Europe +14%
Greater China +11%
Japan + 26%
Rest of Asia Pacific + 17%
In terms of revenue sequential change:
Americas + 52%
Europe + 62%
Greater China +83%
Japan + 88%
Rest of Asia Pacific +144%
The figures show that Asia is the fastest-growing sector in terms of growth in the medium term. In the short term they are very much the fastest-growing sector in terms of growth. Much of this huge accelerating growth short term is caused by the impact of the iPhone X. However it is backed up by the full product portfolio.
In terms of net sales, China now represents 20.3%. Japan represents 8.2%. Rest of Asia Pacific represents 7.8%. That gives Asia 36.3% of total net sales for the company.
Q1 2018 Analyst Call On the analyst call , executives placed more emphasis on Asia than they had in the past with certain key comments.
The iPhone X lead the charge in the region, but it was not just this model. This was despite negative calls by some analysts. As CEO Tim Cook stated:
"In urban China ...the top five smartphones last quarter were all iPhones...In Japan six of the seven were iPhones."
As for the iPad, rumors of its death have been somewhat exaggerated. As Tim Cook said:
"In China, new and switching users made up over 70% of all iPad sales."
So the product has a new lease of life there. Elsewhere, iPad enjoyed double-digit growth in India, Japan, Australia and Korea.
As for the Mac, Cook contrasted:
"Worldwide 60% of our Mac sales were to first-time buyers and switchers and in China that number was almost 90%....We grew market share for iPhone in the quarter but we also grew share in iPad and Mac during the quarter and wearables were extremely strong."
He pointed out also that although China numbers showed an 11% increase for Greater China, if one took this on an average weekly revenue basis, the numbers were up 19%. Double-digit revenue growth for a second quarter in a row hardly ties in with the picture some had tried to paint of a decline in China. It is true that forecasts indicate a difficult year for mobile phone volumes in general in China in 2018. These may or may not turn out to be accurate. However there is no reason to suppose Apple won't increase its market share.
Other new product developments hold out great promise for Apple in Asia.
In a continent where cashless payment is increasingly king, Apple Pay continues to move ahead. As Cook exampled:
"Today you can use Apple Pay to take a subway in Guangzhou."
This is despite the very well-entrenched cashless payments already on tap in the country. In Singapore Apple Pay also is being extended to the MRT and bus systems there, as just one example. The company also is cooperating with local rivals. It announced just recently that it will now accept " Alipay, " the system from Alibaba (NYSE: BABA ) in its stores in China. Previously it had accepted "Alipay" on its digital stores. In a way the company had little option but to cooperate with the world's largest mobile as an online payments platform.
Augmented reality is very big in China as well, and this fits well with Cook's enthusiasm for it. As he stated:
"I am a huge, huge believer in AR. We put a lot of energy on AR moving very fast."
Cook is wise to emphasize this. Chinese heavyweight companies Alibaba, Baidu (NASDAQ: BIDU ) and Tencent ( OTCPK:TCEHY ) all have substantial mobile AR initiatives under way. These are not just in the world of gaming (inspired by Pokemon "Go") but involve tourism, education, healthcare and entertainment.
The situation with home automation is similar in China and elsewhere in Asia. Governments in the region worry about increased labour costs and ponder how to enable "smart cities." The Apple "Home Pod" is likely to be greeted positively in the region.
As my article in September last year detailed, the new products from Apple seem to be perfectly geared to appeal to Asian consumers. Brand loyalty and mobile lifestyles are paramount.
Apple's well-known halo effect where the iPhone leads into the whole Apple infrastructure is taking off around the region. This just replicates what was seen in North America, Europe and Japan in the past.
China - Looking Ahead Tim Cook has shown that he is in China for the long term. He also has shown that he's willing to cooperate with the Chinese government and make compromises where necessary.
Apple's first data center in the country was set up at Guizhou, at a cost of US $1billion. A second data center at Ulanqab in Mongolia is now set to open in 2020.
The iPhone will continue to lead the charge. Those observers who over the years state that iPhones will be too expensive for the Chinese market have been proved wrong time and again. Last year as Counterpoint reports , the iPhone 7 Plus was the second best selling model in the country, only just below the much cheaper Oppo R95. The iPhone 7 was the fifth best seller.
Worldwide Appl e outsold its biggest competitor Samsung (OTCMKTS: OTC:SSNLF ) in 2017. Its Korean rival has been hit by a lack of excitement in its new models. Similarly Chinese manufacturers have been waxing and waning. Huawei, Oppo, Vivo and One Plus have all seen sales decline after an initial surge in their new low-cost models. Each one was previously cited by some analysts as sounding a potential death-knell for the iPhone in the country.
According to reports from Kantar, the iPhone was the top-selling model in China in the last quarter of 2017. Canalys came out with a figure of 7 million sold in China in the last quarter of 2017 out of 29 million sold worldwide. These are just the latest datapoints illustrating the way in which expensive iPhones are able to sell well in China. The iOS market share in China rose 10.1%.
The currency equation also seems to be finally turning in Apple's favor in China. The renminbi is at a three-year low against the US dollar. The past strength of the US dollar has enabled Apple to invest more cheaply in the country. Now a weaker US dollar improves Apple's US dollar profitability in its ever more important overseas markets. The U.S. government policy on the dollar is incoherent but it seems likely Trump himself wants a cheap dollar policy which will benefit Apple's profit figures.
Exact sales figures for the Apple Watch are not broken down by the company. It is generally considered though that sales are very strong in China, as I detailed here . China already is the world's leading marke t for watch sales. The new Watch 3 has had some teething problems due to lack of LTE connectivity of the new eSIM chip, but this is only a short-term problem.
Elsewhere in Asia luxury watches are big business. For instance Singapore, a very small country, is nevertheless the world's tenth largest watch market. Local telecoms company Singtel is now providing built-in cellular service for the new Watch 3. Australia, Hong Kong and Japan are up and running. Others will follow suit within the next few months.
On the back of this Apple's health applications such as "Health Kit" and "Research Kit" and the open-source "Care Kit" should resonate strongly in the region. They tie in with various Chinese Government initiatives in this regard. The wearables market is set to boom in Asia and especially in China, as I detailed in an article in June last year.
Rest of Asia - Looking Ahead The growing population of Asia, its youth dynamic beloved of economists and the region's GDP growth means Asia will only become more important in the short term, in the medium term, and in the long term.
There are 4.3 billion people in Asia. This represents 60% of the world's population. Currently it is only 34% of the world's GDP. Its percentage share though is growing rapidly. The graphic below illustrates world economic GDP activity as calculated by the World Bank.

Asia's 34% of world GDP contrasts with 28% for North America and 21% for Europe. Its lead in share of world economic GDP will only increase as its economies and demographics are favourable. This shows up clearly in IMF forecasts. GDP growth figures going forward for all countries in Asia can be viewed in the IMF projections here. 
Apple's recent increasing reliance on Asia is only set to increase on the basis of the above data. Many of the benefits in China apply elsewhere in Asia.
Amongst these is Apple's build-up of stores in the region. They have been somewhat late to do this, as I have written about previously. Asia represents 36.3% of total net sales for the company but has only 11% of worldwide stores. Now they seem finally to be making up for lost time.
The latest plan is for a huge "global flagship store" in Melbourne. This will be only the fifth such store worldwide. There are currently 22 stores in China where iOS market share grew 1.2% in the final quarter of the year. New stores have recently opened in Singapore (said to be the second busiest in the world), Bangkok and Seoul.
Japan meanwhile continues to be the standout market for Apple in Asia, and perhaps worldwide. It was no surprise that the iPhone X jumped to being the best-selling model in the country with an 18.2% market share. The second best selling phone in the country was the iPhone 8. Last year over half of all mobile phones sold in the country were from Apple. 46% of tablets sold in the country are iPads. An earlier article of mine detailed the great depth of the Apple brand in the country where iOS market share is over 50%.
Apple Pay has been flourishing there on the transit systems, despite the already advanced state of contactless payment in Japan. It is integrated with the Osaifu Keitai mobile wallet system which you see everywhere in the country. The company is driving its gaming revenue in Japan in conjunction with Nintendo ( OTCMKTS: OTCPK:NTDOY ). This is very likely to be another strong growth stream for apple in the country.
Apple products particularly appeal to the Japanese because of their minimalism and design features. However the market in general is an indication of what Apple could achieve elsewhere in Asia.
Brand loyalty is a major driver to sales all around Asia. This is especially true in the IT space. The three most powerful brands in the Asia Pacific region are Apple, Samsung and Sony (NYSE: SNE ).
India will be a huge driver of future growth in Asia for Apple. I will be covering that big topic in a separate article. India has the potential to be another China story for the company and increase further the vital importance of the region for Asia.
Asia is what makes Apple still very much a potential growth company. Apple's valuation metrics though are very low and certainly not those of a growth company. For instance if you compare Apple to the S&P US BMI Information Technology sector:
PE 16.42 (S&P 31.2).
Price to Forecasted Earnings 13.84 (S&P 21.75).
Price/Sales 3.38 (S&P 4.21).
Price / Tangible Book 6.13 (S&P 6.03)
Price / Cash Flow 14.02 (S&P 18.77).
The latest stock market turmoil only adds to the attractive investment potential in the long run.
Conclusion Apple's growth in Asia is faster than in any other region. The region itself is a faster growing region than any other in the world. Apple's product mix reflect what Asian consumers want. Its increased retail roll-out in the region is important for consumer branding and service.
In my opinion the growing importance of Asia to Apple has been underestimated in many quarters and will only grow.
